university: University of Texas at El Paso

documents.title: UTEP Guidance for Teaching with AI Technologies (Fall 2025: Teaching and Learning in an AI World)
documents.stance_why: The document says instructors may 'fully embrace AI in your course, allow limited use, or prohibit it altogether' and supplies five sample syllabus statements (free use, with acknowledgement, early stages, with permission, not permitted), so it sets no stance itself and offers tiers.
tiers: AI for Brainstorming or Early Stages
documents.summary: Provost guidance leaves the AI decision to each instructor, urging them to explain their rationale and set transparent boundaries. It supplies five sample syllabus statements and a three-level per-assignment framework, and refers misuse to Community Standards under existing integrity policy. A second half offers student-facing best practices on disclosure, verification, ownership and data privacy.

units.why: The opening says faculty may 'fully embrace AI in your course, allow limited use, or prohibit it altogether', so the stance is left to each instructor; this is per-instructor choice (P04).
units.anchor: fully embrace AI in your course, allow limited use, or prohibit it altogether

units.why: The sentence tells instructors to 'communicate your rationale clearly' and set 'fair and transparent boundaries'; it is about giving reasons to students, so P66 fits better than P09 (which needs a syllabus statement).
units.anchor: communicate your rationale clearly, establish fair and transparent boundaries
units.policy: Instructors communicate their rationale clearly, establish fair and transparent boundaries, and foster student ownership of learning in an AI-enhanced world.
units.fit_note: Also asks for fair and transparent boundaries and student ownership, which P66 does not capture.

units.why: The guidance offers 'ready-to-use syllabus language, guiding questions, and adaptable frameworks', i.e. templates for instructors (P110).
units.anchor: ready-to-use syllabus language, guiding questions, and adaptable frameworks

units.why: The line ties AI use to 'your course learning outcomes', so the stance should follow learning objectives (P83).
units.anchor: help you align AI use with your course learning outcomes

units.why: The university 'encourage[s] faculty to integrate' AI 'thoughtfully and transparently'; a positive institutional stance toward AI in teaching, so P02 rather than P56.
units.anchor: we encourage faculty to integrate Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies thoughtfully and transparently

units.why: States AI can enrich the classroom only 'to enhance-not replace-student thinking'; a condition that AI not replace thinking, so P32.
units.anchor: enhance—not replace—student thinking, creativity, and ownership of learning

units.why: 'Regardless of your approach' instructors 'should' tell students the why; sharing the reason behind the rule is P66.
units.anchor: Communicate your rationale governing your AI stance clearly. Share the “why” with students.

units.why: Instructors 'should' 'Establish fair and transparent boundaries' whatever their stance; an expectation to apply rules transparently, P124.
units.anchor: Establish fair and transparent boundaries.

units.why: Instructors should build 'reflective and iterative practices' so students 'think deeply about their processes'; a course-design move around AI, P35.
units.anchor: cultivating reflective and iterative practices that challenge students to think deeply about their processes
units.policy: Instructors foster student ownership of learning in an AI-enhanced world by cultivating reflective and iterative practices that challenge students to think deeply about their processes.
units.fit_note: Describes pedagogical practices in general terms, not a specific redesign.

units.why: The guiding question asks whether the instructor's stance aligns 'with my course learning outcomes', reinforcing P83.
units.anchor: How does my stance on AI align with my course learning outcomes?

units.why: Asks instructors to turn the policy 'into a learning conversation rather than a restriction', i.e. discuss it with students, P66.
units.anchor: How might I turn my AI policy into a learning conversation rather than a restriction?

units.why: Suggests adding 'scaffolds (practice, reflection, citation)' to make AI use transparent; assignment redesign around AI, P35.
units.anchor: What scaffolds (practice, reflection, citation) can I add to make AI use transparent

units.why: 'This isn't about surveillance! The goal is not to catch AI misuse' says policing is not the aim, nearest P60 (decline to police) though it frames the aim as cultivating responsible use.
units.anchor: The goal is not to “catch” AI misuse but rather to cultivate responsible
units.fit_note: Frames the aim as cultivating responsible use rather than stating that no policing will occur.

units.why: 'Clear expectations reduce confusion' gives the reason for communicating rules; it is a rationale for explaining expectations, P66.
units.anchor: Clear expectations reduce confusion and help students develop discernment to make ethical choices

units.why: Instructors are to 'Model curiosity and critical evaluation', showing when to seek help or question results; P112 (instructors model responsible use) is nearest.
units.anchor: Model curiosity and critical evaluation to demonstrate that being a learner
units.fit_note: The modeling is of learner habits generally, not explicitly of the instructor's own AI use.

units.why: The grade 'will belong to the student, not the AI program' means students own what they submit, P29.
units.anchor: they must take complete responsibility for its content

units.why: 'AI cannot reproduce critical thought, reflection, or personal insights' says AI must not replace human thinking, closest to P32.
units.anchor: AI cannot reproduce critical thought, reflection, or personal insights.

units.why: Instructors should discuss 'falsified information and references, which generative AI content often includes'; this warns that AI output can be fabricated, P31.
units.anchor: Discuss with students the ethical as well as practical ramifications of using falsified information

units.why: Instructors should 'Define which assignments or process stages explicitly prohibit AI use', which is per-assignment rule-setting, P04.
units.anchor: Define which assignments or process stages explicitly prohibit AI use.

units.why: The section says it is 'important to outline what constitutes AI misuse in your course and to make clear the consequences'; stating how misuse is handled is P123.
units.anchor: outline what constitutes AI misuse in your course and to make clear the consequences

units.why: 'Clarify that violations fall under UTEP's existing academic integrity policies' treats AI misuse as an integrity violation under existing policy, P36.
units.anchor: Clarify that violations fall under UTEP’s existing academic integrity policies.

units.why: 'Inform students that academic misuse of AI will be directed to the Office of Community Standards' names the formal referral route, P81.
units.anchor: academic misuse of AI will be directed to the Office of Community Standards

units.why: The 'Free Use of AI' statement says AI 'is freely permitted' and users 'are encouraged to explore', a default-permit and encourage template, P02.
units.anchor: AI use is freely permitted in this class. You are encouraged to explore
units.fit_note: Sample syllabus statement offered as one option for instructors.

units.why: The permit-with-acknowledgement sample requires students to 'describe and acknowledge how you used them with each submission', P24.
units.anchor: you must describe and acknowledge how you used them with each submission

units.why: The same sample says 'Any uncredited AI-generated content will be treated as plagiarism and referred to the Office of Community Standards': nondisclosure is itself the violation, P28.
units.anchor: Any uncredited AI-generated content will be treated as plagiarism and referred
units.frag_start: You are welcome to use AI tools to support
units.fit_note: Also routes the case to Community Standards (P36/P81).

units.why: The sample says students 'may use AI tools to brainstorm ideas or plan your approach', a permitted use, P15.
units.anchor: You may use AI tools to brainstorm ideas or plan your approach.
units.frag_start: You may use AI tools to brainstorm

units.why: 'your final work must reflect your own reasoning and analysis' requires submitted work to be the student's own, P29.
units.anchor: your final work must reflect your own reasoning and analysis

units.why: 'AI-generated ideas are not your own and must be cited if directly included' requires citation of AI content, P24.
units.anchor: AI-generated ideas are not your own and must be cited

units.why: 'You may use AI tools only with prior instructor approval' makes use contingent on approval, P107.
units.anchor: You may use AI tools only with prior instructor approval.
units.frag_start: You may use AI tools only

units.why: If approved, students 'include a brief note ... describing how you used the tool and cite the tool properly', which includes citing the tool, P25.
units.anchor: include a brief note in your submission describing how you used the tool
units.fit_note: Requires a description of use and a proper citation of the tool, not the prompt or output.

units.why: The 'Not Permitted' sample says 'Use of AI technologies is not permitted in this course', a course-level ban, P01.
units.anchor: Use of AI technologies is not permitted in this course.
units.frag_start: Use of AI technologies is not

units.why: The sample gives the reason: it 'ensures that your work demonstrates your own learning and critical thinking', a skill-building rationale, P41.
units.anchor: This policy ensures that your work demonstrates your own learning and critical thinking.

units.why: 'Any identified AI-generated content will be treated as plagiarism' classifies banned AI use as plagiarism, P36.
units.anchor: Any identified AI-generated content will be treated as plagiarism

units.why: The guidance points to a Vanderbilt compilation of syllabus statements, a pointer to further examples, P115.
units.anchor: For more examples, please see this resource from Vanderbilt University

units.why: 'Students are more likely to respect AI boundaries when they understand why' is a reason for explaining rules, P66.
units.anchor: Students are more likely to respect AI boundaries when they understand why those boundaries exist.

units.why: Instructors should 'pair it with your learning goals for the assignment and express your rationale' for each assignment, P66.
units.anchor: pair it with your learning goals for the assignment and express your rationale
units.frag_start: When you introduce your AI policy

units.why: 'Yes, and here's how' is a named per-assignment level: free use with acknowledgement, prompt documentation and reflective evaluation, P05.
units.anchor: AI may be used freely with transparent acknowledgement, documentation of prompts
units.fit_note: Also requires prompt documentation and reflective evaluation (P26).

units.why: 'Sometimes, and here's when' is the second named level: AI in specific stages, 'brainstorming, outlining, and editing', P05.
units.anchor: AI may be used in specific stages of course projects: brainstorming, outlining, and editing.
units.frag_start: AI may be used in specific
units.fit_note: Lists brainstorming, outlining and editing as the permitted stages.

units.why: 'No, and here's why' is the third level, with a skill-based reason template ('would prevent you from practicing ___ skill'), P05.
units.anchor: AI use is not permitted because it would prevent you from practicing _______ skill.
units.frag_start: AI use is not permitted because

units.why: The line credits the three-statement framework to an outside author and names its purposes ('transparency, fairness, and student judgment'); no type covers provenance of a framework, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: promotes transparency, fairness, and student judgment
units.uncovered_note: Attributes the three-statement framework to an outside source and names its purposes.

units.why: Section 2 says it is 'our responsibility to help students engage with these technologies ethically, transparently, and with critical judgment', a general ethical expectation with little specific content, P116.
units.anchor: it’s our responsibility to help students engage with these technologies ethically

units.why: 'AI-powered tools are becoming integral to academic, professional, and creative environments' is professional-relevance rationale, P44.
units.anchor: AI-powered tools are becoming integral to academic, professional, and creative environments.

units.why: Principles help students 'Recognize how AI can support-not replace-human thought', P32.
units.anchor: Recognize how AI can support—not replace—human thought, creativity, and collaboration

units.why: Principles also ask students to 'Make intentional choices about when and how to engage with AI', i.e. weigh use in context, P118.
units.anchor: Make intentional choices about when and how to engage with AI

units.why: Section 2 restates that if AI 'makes logical errors' the grade belongs to the student; coded because it adds the point that AI errors are the student's problem, nearest P31 (AI output can be wrong).
units.anchor: generates content that does not adhere to the assignment, makes logical errors
units.frag_start: That means that if the AI program
units.fit_note: Stresses that AI errors become the student's grade, also P29.

units.why: 'Use AI to learn, not to shortcut learning' allows brainstorming, outlining, clarifying but requires own voice; skill-building rationale, P41.
units.anchor: Use AI to learn, not to shortcut learning
units.fit_note: Also lists permitted uses (brainstorming, outlining, clarifying) and requires own voice and reasoning (P32).

units.why: 'Be transparent about your use' tells students to be upfront and follow the instructor's rule on citing or disclosing it, P24.
units.anchor: If you use AI to help you with an assignment, be upfront.

units.why: 'Don't accept AI responses at face value. Always fact-check' is a verification duty, P31.
units.anchor: Don't accept AI responses at face value. Always fact-check,

units.why: 'Don't pass off AI-generated content as your original work unless allowed' bars submitting AI output as one's own, P19.
units.anchor: Don’t pass off AI-generated content as your original work unless allowed.

units.why: 'Follow the ground rules of each assignment' makes students follow assignment-level rules, P78.
units.anchor: Follow the ground rules of each assignment
units.fit_note: Gives the reason that some activities prohibit AI to develop critical thinking or communication skills (P41).

units.why: 'Struggle and reflection are part of developing mastery' justifies limiting AI use by skill-building, P41.
units.anchor: Struggle and reflection are part of developing mastery.

units.why: 'Avoid entering personal, sensitive, or proprietary information into AI tools' is a data-protection rule, P50.
units.anchor: Avoid entering personal, sensitive, or proprietary information into AI tools.

notes: Only one included document. Sample statements are templates offered to instructors, so unit actors reflect who each line addresses.
